title: Search Open Technical Databases
summary: Rather than sending a single packet, this technique consults third party collections of technical facts about the victim: domain registration records, certificate transparency logs, historical and passive domain name system records, routing data, internet wide scan datasets and internet of things search services. The attraction is that these repositories are free, already populated, and reveal history that live probing cannot recover, such as former hosting providers, retired subdomains and certificates issued for internal looking names. The adversary correlates them to reconstruct infrastructure, identify who hosts and protects the target, and spot weak points such as an expired certificate, a typo squatted service or an asset pointing at a decommissioned address. Because the queries go to the data provider rather than the victim, victim side telemetry is usually absent, and the practical controls are data governance ones: keep registration details accurate, understand what your certificates and domain name system records publish, and monitor for impersonating lookalike registrations. This complements active scanning, which confirms what the databases suggest.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker uses public technical records to learn about you. These records describe your domain names, certificates, address ranges and past hosting. They are kept by registries and community projects, and anyone can read them.
beginner.whyItMatters: These records are free and need no contact with your systems. They also hold history, so an attacker can find names and addresses you stopped using years ago. Old records often point to systems nobody maintains any more. Your own logs will not show the search at all.
howItWorks: The attacker looks up who registered your domain names and which name servers answer for them.
They read certificate records, which list the names a certificate was issued for.
They review historical name lookups to find subdomains and addresses you used before.
They pull internet wide scan data to see which ports and services were seen on your addresses.
They compare providers and network ranges to find hosting, mail and protection services.
They combine everything into an infrastructure map and pick the weakest, least maintained point.
beginner.example: Think of a town hall that keeps an open ledger of every shop, its owner and its previous addresses. Anyone can read the ledger and see that a shop moved twice and left an empty unit behind. The attacker never visits the town, yet they know which abandoned unit to try first.
takeaways: Public records carry history, so retired domains and addresses still leak information.
Keep registration contacts and certificate names accurate and review them regularly.
Monitor for lookalike domain registrations that reuse your naming style.

objectives: Name the main open technical databases relevant to reconnaissance.
Explain what domain registration and certificate transparency records reveal.
Describe how passive and historical domain name system data exposes retired infrastructure.
Explain why this collection is largely invisible in victim side telemetry.
Suggest governance steps that limit information exposed through public records.
